title: Explainable Adaptive Continuous Authentication for Smart Healthcare: Exact Inline Attribution and a Clinical Safety Valve Under Zero Trust
content: Healthcare has led every industry in average breach cost for more than a decade, and the largest recent incidents in the sector began with credentials that were valid at entry and were never re-verified afterwards. Continuous authentication targets that failure, but the literatures that could supply it are each incomplete: reinforcement-learning risk engines adapt without justifying their decisions, explainable-AI authentication explains only after the fact, and neither prices the cost of obstructing a clinician, which in a clinical setting is a patient-safety event rather than a usability nuisance. This paper presents the Hybrid Explainable Adaptive Authentication Framework (HEAAF), a zero-trust policy engine that produces an exact attribution inside the decision cycle and carries patient safety as an explicit policy term. HEAAF is evaluated by simulation: the behavioural channel is the real CMU keystroke-dynamics benchmark under a genuine template-ageing split, coupled to a documented clinical context generator supplying six labelled attack scenarios with ground-truth driver sets and hard negatives, with every policy read at a matched 1% clinical friction budget over eight seeds. Three results follow. Grouping makes exactness affordable: sixteen evidence features partition into eight semantic groups, so exact group Shapley values cost 28 = 256 coalition evaluations in one batched pass, and a complete decision with an exact justification takes 0.611ms against 1.214ms for the same decision explained by approximate integrated gradients; we further show that summing feature attributions into groups is not the group Shapley value and that the two disagree on the dominant factor once in eight decisions. An explicit clinical safety valve removes emergency denials outright, from 1.10% to 0.000% for a G mean cost of 0.005, and the graded escalation ladder delivers the same detection for 7.6 rather than 26.5 clinician-hours of annual friction. Contrary to our starting hypothesis the reinforcement learning risk score is not the strongest detector: a supervised detector in the same policy engine gains 0.378 G-mean, which relocates the contribution of reinforcement learning to the graded action policy. Code, seeds and the scripts that regenerate every reported number are released.
